newsitem.title: USA: Class status hoped for in Hooters suit.
newsitem.headline: Class status hoped for in Hooters suit.

text.p: Attorneys for a former employee at Hooters of America Inc who has filed a sexual harassment suit against the restaurant chain said Tuesday they hoped that publicizing the suit would attract additional plaintiffs for a class action.

"I am here today on behalf of myself and any other Hooters employees who feel that they have been abused," Annette Phillips, a former waitress and bartender at the privately held Atlanta-based company, who brought the suit, told a news conference.
"I was a good employee and I understood that the job required me to wear shorts and t-shirts, but in return Hooters promised to protect me," she said.

Thomas Henderson, an attorney with the Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, and counsel for the proposed class, said he did not know how many people might eventually become eligible to join the class.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court, District of South Carolina, does not seek specific monetary damages.
Phillips worked as a waitress and bartender at Hooters from May 1989 until June 1996, when she left, claiming she could no longer bear working conditions at the restaurant in Myrtle Beach, S.C..

Among other things, Phillips said a male manager had pulled his shorts and exposed himself to her. But in a statement read to the news conference, Phillips said the worst experience was at the hands of a relative of a company executive, "who slapped and grabbed my rear end," while she was working as a bartender.

She said the restaurant's manager had advised her not to pursue the case and that, after she left her job and contacted a lawyer, Hooters responded by suing her, in turn prompting the countersuit announced Tuesday.

Phillips and her lawyers argued that Hooters requires its employees to sign an agreement in which they give up their rights to defend themselves against sexual harassment. Among other things, they said Hooters requires that harassment complaints be submitted to an arbitration panel whose members are chosen only from a list approved by Hooters.

Founded in 1982, Hooters is a $350 million restaurant chain with locations in 38 states, Canada, Puerto Rico and Singapore. Its outlets are best known for their female waitresses and bartenders, who wear very short orange shorts and small white t-shirts.

The federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission last year decided not to file a sex discrimination suit against the restaurant chain, which mounted a $1 milion publicity campaign last fall to keep from hiring male members of its all-female wait staff of "Hooters Girls."
The EEOC has asked the court in South Carolina to allow it to enter the case as a friend of the court.
A spokesman for Hooters said he did not have an immediate response from the company, but hoped to have one shortly.
